title: Status of flora in Nepal and world representation
topicTitle: Status of flora in Nepal and world representation
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Where Nepal's Plants Stand in the World

This topic answers a simple question with a striking answer: **how much of the world's plant life does Nepal hold, and why?** Nepal occupies only **0.1% of Earth's land area** yet carries a disproportionate share of global plant diversity — the result of its position at the collision of two biogeographic realms and its vertical compression of almost every climate zone on Earth.

- **Why it matters:** conservation (Unit 10), vegetation types and every "economic importance" question in this unit depend on knowing what grows here and how it compares globally.
- **Key idea to carry:** altitude is Nepal's "latitude" — climbing from the Terai to the summit crosses the equivalent of tropical to polar zones within ~200 km.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts — What "Flora" and "Representation" Mean

**Flora** = the plant life of a given region or period. **Floristic representation** = how a region's plant diversity compares with the world's — measured by species counts, endemism and share of global totals.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Species richness | Number of species in an area |
| **Endemic species** | Found only in that region and nowhere else on Earth |
| Biodiversity hotspot | Region with exceptional endemism under severe threat |
| Phytogeographic realm | A large region sharing a characteristic flora (e.g. Indo-Malayan, Palaearctic) |
| Vegetation zone | Belt of characteristic plant life, here set mainly by altitude |

## 3. Nepal's Flora — The Numbers

| Group | Approximate species in Nepal | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Flowering plants (angiosperms) | ~6,000–7,000 | The richest group; Nepal holds about 2–3% of the world's flowering plants |
| Gymnosperms | ~30+ species | Including *Tsuga*, *Abies*, *Picea* in the high conifer forests |
| Ferns and fern allies (pteridophytes) | ~500–600 | Rich because of moist monsoon forests |
| Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) | ~1,100+ | Very high for the country's size |
| Lichens | ~500+ | Sensitive pollution indicators |
| Algae and fungi | Thousands | incompletely catalogued |

**Endemism:** a substantial share of Nepal's flowering plants (~300+ species) are endemic to the Himalaya — products of isolation on young mountains.

### 3.1 Why Nepal is so rich — the four reasons (the conceptual core)

1. **Altitudinal range:** the country rises from ~60 m (Terai, Kechana Kalan) to 8,848 m (Everest) — a vertical span that packs tropical, subtropical, temperate, subalpine, alpine and nival zones into ~200 km of horizontal distance.
2. **Meeting of two realms:** Nepal sits at the junction of the **Palaearctic** (Holarctic) and **Indo-Malayan** biogeographic realms, so species of both mingle here.
3. **Monsoon climate:** the summer monsoon delivers most of Nepal's precipitation, sustaining dense forests and epiphyte-rich vegetation.
4. **Complex topography and microclimates:** deep valleys, rain shadows (Mustang, Manang) and south–north slope contrasts create countless isolated habitats — each a speciation workshop.

### 3.2 Altitudinal vegetation zones (memorise the sequence)

| Zone | Approximate altitude | Characteristic vegetation |
|---|---|---|
| Subtropical | up to ~1,000 m | Sal (*Shorea robusta*) forest, Terai grasslands |
| Lower temperate | 1,000–2,000 m | Pine (*Pinus roxburghii*), Schima–Castanopsis forest |
| Upper temperate | 2,000–3,000 m | Oak (*Quercus*), rhododendron forest |
| Subalpine | 3,000–4,000 m | Birch (*Betula*), fir (*Abies*), juniper, rhododendron scrub |
| Alpine | 4,000–5,000 m | Grasses, sedges, cushion plants, *Rhododendron anthopogon* |
| Nival | above ~5,000 m | Lichens, mosses, no flowering plants beyond snowline |

## 4. Nepal's Flora in World Representation

| Comparison | Figure |
|---|---|
| Nepal's share of world land area | ~0.1% |
| Nepal's share of world flowering plants | ~2–3% |
| Nepal's position among Asian countries | Among the top for species-per-area density |
| Himalaya as a whole | One of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots (the Himalaya hotspot) |
| Protected coverage | National parks, reserves and conservation areas protect representative vegetation of every zone (details in Unit 10) |

**Conceptual framing:** richness per unit area — not absolute totals — is what makes Nepal globally significant. A temperate country the size of Nepal in Europe or North America would hold far fewer species.

## 5. Threats to This Flora (bridge to conservation)

1. Deforestation for agriculture, fuelwood and timber.
2. Overgrazing and encroachment of grasslands and wetlands.
3. Invasive alien species (e.g. *Chromolaena odorata*, *Mikania micrantha* — "banmara").
4. Climate change shifting vegetation zones upward faster than species can migrate.
5. Unsustainable harvesting of medicinal and aromatic plants (yarsagumba, jatamansi).

## 6. Conceptual Relationships

- **Here → vegetation (Unit 5):** the zone table above becomes the vegetation-types classification.
- **Here → conservation (Unit 10):** endemism and threat status justify national parks and species programmes.
- **Here → ecological adaptation (Unit 4):** each vegetation zone is an adaptation story (xerophytes in rain shadows, hydrophytes in wetlands).
- **Here → Unit 2 topics:** the fungi, algae, bryophytes, ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms you study next are exactly the groups counted in Nepal's flora.

## 7. Exam Orientation

### 7.1 Previous year questions

No dedicated question on Nepal's flora status appears in the authored solved-paper bank (2021–2024). The questions below are **NEB-style practice**, clearly distinguished from verified PYQs.

### 7.2 NEB-style practice questions with model answers

**Q1 (3m) — Why is Nepal rich in flora despite its small area?**
Answer: (1) Extreme **altitudinal range** (60 m → 8,848 m) packs tropical-to-nival vegetation zones within ~200 km; (2) Nepal lies at the **meeting of two biogeographic realms** (Palaearctic and Indo-Malayan), so species of both occur here; (3) the **monsoon** climate sustains dense, moist forests; (4) **complex topography** creates many microclimates and isolated habitats that promote speciation and endemism.

**Q2 (2m) — What is an endemic species? Why does the Himalaya have many?**
Answer: An endemic species is one confined to a particular region and found nowhere else. The young Himalaya isolated populations on separate valleys and slopes; millions of years of isolation in distinct microclimates produced many species found only here.

**Q3 (2m) — List the major vegetation zones of Nepal in order with one characteristic plant each.**
Answer: Subtropical — Sal (*Shorea robusta*); lower temperate — chir pine (*Pinus roxburghii*); upper temperate — oak–rhododendron; subalpine — birch (*Betula*) and fir (*Abies*); alpine — grasses and sedges; nival — lichens and mosses beyond the snowline.

**Q4 (2m) — Name two invasive plants threatening Nepal's flora and one effect.**
Answer: *Mikania micrantha* (banmara) and *Chromolaena odorata*; they smother native vegetation and tree seedlings, reducing native species diversity in forests and protected areas.

### 7.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Quoting invented precise species totals — give the accepted ranges ("about 6,000–7,000 flowering plants").
2. Calling the whole Himalaya a "national park" — the hotspot designation is different from protected-area categories.
3. Confusing **endemic** (found only here) with **endangered** (at risk of extinction) — a species can be one without the other.
confusion: **Endemic vs endangered:** endemic = geographically restricted to one region; endangered = at high risk of extinction. A species can be endemic and common, or widespread and endangered.
**Flora vs vegetation:** flora is the list of plant species; vegetation is the actual plant cover communities (forest, grassland) on the ground.
**Hotspot vs protected area:** a hotspot is a global scientific designation of high endemism + threat; a protected area is a legal national designation (park, reserve).
